v.why: Replacing a missing final edge with a 3x3 conv adds a whole new learnable path, which gains more than upgrading an existing op.
Reconnecting the input edge with a conv gives a larger gain than swapping one op for another.
Adding a conv on the direct input-to-output edge where none existed gains more than replacing an existing op.
Deleting a 3x3 conv removes a major feature path and costs more than deleting a weak op.
Cutting the conv on the input edge starves downstream edges and hurts accuracy heavily.
Downgrading a 3x3 conv to skip loses far more capacity than replacing a weaker op.
Replacing a conv with pooling on the output edge strongly reduces accuracy.
Activating a dead edge with a conv gives a larger gain than replacing an existing op.
Adding a conv to a missing intermediate edge creates a new deeper path and gains more than a swap.
Replacing a 3x3 conv with skip loses more accuracy than replacing a weak op.

raw:
These hypotheses come from general NAS-Bench-201 knowledge, mainly that convolutions carry most of the accuracy and that removing or downgrading them costs accuracy. The 20 experiments are consistent with this but are too sparse to confirm any single one, so I did not tune the hypotheses to them.
